Urban freeways on weekends have the least data with only three shuttle buses and less than 6 hours of data. On other roads on weekends, there were four buses and 56 hours of data. On weekdays, there were 153 and 615 hours on freeways and other roads, respectively, with five vehicles each. The choice to include these distributions is also complicated by these vehicles likely belonging to one fleet of airport shuttle buses but intending to represent the entire “other bus” source type. However, if EPA views these distributions as an improvement over non-source-specific distributions, they could potentially be added to MOVES. On weekdays, we observe some reasonably characteristic patterns such as a slightly slower peak compared to other source types at 50 mph on urban freeways and a fairly typical broad peak around 10 mph on other roads. On weekends, we see a similar—if less smooth—trend with a peak at 10 mph on other roads. However, the weekend urban freeways category is quite choppy with a minor and major peak at 35 and 45 mph, respectively, which is not characteristic of freeway behaviors observed in other source types. 57 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. We observe a peak in the speed distribution that is shifted slightly faster than other source types for urban other roads at 15 mph, but otherwise resembles the broad low-speed peak typical for this road type. If—despite the low vehicle count and lack of diverse fleets—having a school-bus-specific speed distribution is advantageous over non-source-specific defaults, this distribution could be considered for inclusion in MOVES.
